title: Lab 2 – Acromegaly, prolactinoma, hypopituitarism, DI
html:
Source: LP 2.pdf – 14 pages

Acromegaly and Gigantism- causes #1

  • 1. GH-Secreting/Mixt GH-PRL Secreting Pituitary Adenoma
  • !! Acromegaly and gigantism are virtually always secondary to a pituitary adenoma.
  • !! Genetic syndromes associated with pituitary tumors and GH hypersecretion:
  • - MEN 1 (Werner syndrome): pituitary adenoma+ primary hyperparathyroidism+
  • pancreatic neuroendocrine tumors
  • - McCune Albright syndrome
  • - Carney complex
  • - Familial isolated pituitary adenomas (FIPA)- characterized by genetic defects in the
  • AIP gene (tumor suppressor gene).
  • 2. Paraneoplastic Secretion of GHRH-Like (e.g. carcinoid, islet cell tumor, lung
  • carcinoma)/GH-Like Substances (e.g. islet cell tumor, non-Hodgkin’s lymphoma)
  • Acromegaly and Gigantism- clinical picture
  • A) Effects of GH/IGF-1 hypersecretion
  • Gigantism
  • 1. Tall stature: height ~ 200-240 cm (>3 DS), US/LS~1
  • 2. Visceromegaly
  • Acromegaly
  • 1. Acrofacial dysmorphism and skin changes:
  • - Prominence of the supraorbital ridges and frontal bossing, enlargement of the nose,
  • prognathism, dental problems (teeth separation, malocclusion, overbite)
  • - Coarsening of the features, deep nasolabial furrows, macroglossia (tongue) and
  • macrocheilia (lips)
  • - Hands and feet- large, thickened, and bulky, with blunt fingers and toes
  • - Generalized thickening of the skin (e.g. scalp- cutis verticis gyrata), acne/ sebaceous
  • cysts, hyperhidrosis, hypertrichosis, acanthosis nigricans (axillae and neck).
  • 2. Articular, Muscular and Neural Manifestations:
  •  Acromegalic arthropathy (due to bone and cartilage overgrowth):
  • -arthralgias
  • -degenerative arthritis of the spine, hips, and knees (in long-standing cases)-> deformity
  • (e.g. dorsal kyphosis*).
  • *The association between dorsal kyphosis and sternal prominence- Polichinelle sign
  •  Carpal tunnel syndrome (due to neural enlargement and wrist tissue swelling)-painful
  • median nerve compression+ acroparesthesias.
  •  Proximal myopathy- fatigue, myalgias and muscular cramps.

3. Respiratory Manifestations #2

  •  Sleep apnea -snoring, apnea/hypopnea episodes during sleep, daytime sleepiness,
  • morning headache (due to prognathism, thick lips, macroglossia and hypertrophied
  • nasopharyngeal structures that may obstruct airways).
  •  Sonorous deepening of voice (laryngeal hypertrophy+ enlarged paranasal sinuses)
  • 4. Gastrointestinal Features:
  •  Constipation (megacolon)-> rectal prolapse (due to many years of strain).
  •  Increased risk of colonic polyps and colonic carcinoma.
  • 5. Cardiovascular Manifestations
  • - Arterial hypertension (due to water and sodium retention)
  • - Left ventricular hypertrophy
  • - Valvopathies and arrhythmias
  • - Complex cardiomyopathy (in long standing cases): concentric hypertrophy with
  • diastolic dysfunction-> cardiac enlargement-> progressive systolic impairment-> heart
  • failure.
  • 6. Generalized Visceromegaly
  •  Thyromegaly and enlargement of the salivary glands- clinically evident
  •  Hepatomegaly, splenomegaly, renomegaly, cardiomegaly- usually seen on an
  • ultrasound.
  • 7. Other Endocrine and Metabolic Abnormalities
  •  Diffuse or nodular goiter
  •  Diabetes mellitus /impaired glucose tolerance (IGT).
  • 8. Systemic Manifestations:
  •  Lethargy or fatigue
  •  Weight gain
  •  Depression.
  • B) Effects of PRL hypersecretion (mixt adenoma/ hiperPRL due to pituitary stalk compression)
  • • In women
  • - Galactorrhea: spontaneous/induced, permanent/intermittent
  • - Menstrual disorders: Primary/secondary amenorrhea/ Oligomenorrhea
  • - Infertility
  • - Estrogen deficiency symptoms : reduced vaginal lubrication, long-term risk of ↓ bone
  • mineral density (BMD) (osteopenia/osteoporosis).
  • • In men
  • - Low libido is the initial symptom
  • - Erectile dysfunction
  • - Gynecomastia, galactorrhea—exceptional
  • - Infertility.

C) Mass effects #3

  • a) Pituitary tumor syndrome
  •  Headache
  •  Diplopia, ophthalmoplegia, palpebral ptosis
  •  Visual field defects
  •  Hypopituitarism
  • b) Pituitary stalk syndrome
  •  Hyperprolactinemia
  •  Hypopituitarism
  •  Diabetes insipidus
  • Acromegaly and Gigantism- complications
  • 1. Cardiovascular and cerebrovascular diseases
  • 2. Sleep apnea
  • 3. Acromegalic arthropathy with progressive cosmetic deformity and disabling degenerative
  • arthritis
  • 4. Colonic cancer
  • 5. Neurologic complications: carpal tunnel syndrome
  • 6. Kidney stones
  • 7. Diabetes mellitus
  • Acromegaly and Gigantism- investigations
  • 1. Hormonal findings
  •  Basal GH- usually increased but single, random measurements are not entirely reliable,
  • because GH secretion is episodic in acromegaly and because other conditions may ↑ GH
  • secretion-> dynamic tests are needed-> suppression with oral glucose is the simplest
  • and most specific dynamic test for acromegaly
  •  OGTT- in healthy subjects -> ↓ of the GH level to <0.4 ng/ml at 60 min (in acromegaly-
  • GH> 0.4 ng/ml)
  • !! If the patient has diabetes mellitus the 24 h GH mean is used instead- normal response: 24h
  • GH mean< 1 ng/ml (in acromegaly- GH> 1 ng/ml)
  •  IGF-1 ↑
  •  PRL- can be ↑ in mixt adenomas/ hiperPRL due to pituitary stalk compression
  •  Evaluation of the pituitary reserve: FSH, LH, estradiol/testosterone, TSH/FT4,
  • ACTH/cortisol

Acromegaly and Gigantism- investigations #4

  • 2. Other laboratory tests:
  • - Glycemia, HbA1c, total cholesterol, TG
  • - Calcemia, phosphatemia, urinary calcium
  • 3. MRI with contrast (first line)/ CT
  • 4. Visual field assessment
  • 5. Thyroid ultrasound
  • 6. Abdominal ultrasound
  • 7. ECG, echocardiography
  • 8. Colonoscopy
  • 9. Polysomnography
  • Acromegaly and Gigantism- treatment
  • 1. First line of treatment= Surgery
  •  Transsphenoidal Surgery
  •  Craniotomy (when the major suprasellar and lateral extension preclude the
  • transsphenoidal approach)
  • Complications: postoperative hemorrhage, CSF leak, meningitis, visual impairment, transitory
  • diabetes insipidus, hypopituitarism.
  • 2. Second line of treatment= Medical therapy
  •  Somatostatin analogs (inhibit the production of GH)
  • = The therapy of choice for those with residual GH hypersecretion following surgery
  • !! May be used as primary therapy of patients with macroadenoma >2 cm (for 6 months, to
  • reduce the size of the tumor= neoadjuvant) or for patients in whom the risk of surgery or
  • anesthesia= unacceptable (severe sleep apnea/ high-output heart failure).
  •  Somatostatin analogs
  • First generation:
  •  Lanreotide (Somatuline) 30 mg/14 days IM
  •  Lanreotide Autogel® 90–120 mg/month deep SC
  •  Octreotide LAR® (Sandostatin LAR) 10, 20, 40 mg/month IM
  • Side effects: gastrointestinal symptoms, gallstones.
  • Second generation:
  •  Pasireotide (Signifor LAR®) IM 40–60 mg/4 weeks
  • Side effects : patients may develop IGT/ DM+ side effects similar to those caused by first-
  • generation analogs.
  •  DOPA agonists
  •  Cabergoline (Dostinex) 2–4 mg/week

 GH receptor antagonist (competes with endogenous GH for binding to its receptor and #5

  • blocks production of IGF-1)
  •  Pegvisomant (Somavert®) 10–30–40 mg/daily SC
  • Side effects: liver toxicity->monitoring of liver biochemistry= necessary for safety.
  • !! GH levels cannot be used to guide treatment-> IGF-1 is used.
  • !! Serial imaging with MRI scan to evaluate tumor size= recommended.
  •  Replacement therapy (if hypopituitarism is present)
  • 3. Third line of treatment= Radiotherapy
  • • Conventional RT
  • • Gamma knife radiosurgery
  • Complications: hypopituitarism, optochiasmatic arachnoiditis, secondary brain tumors.
  • !! There is a delay in achieving a reduction in GH levels.
  • Hyperprolactinemia- causes
  •  Physiologic: pregnancy, sucking, stress, sleep, exercise
  •  Pharmacologic- e.g. dopamine receptor blockers (haloperidol, metoclopramide),
  • antipsychotics, estrogens, H2 antihistamines, antidepressants
  •  Pathologic
  • 1. Prolactinomas (most common type of pituitary adenoma).
  • 2. Pituitary stalk compression/hypothalamic lesions → functional, “disinhibition
  • hyperprolactinemia.
  • 3. Systemic diseases (primary hypothyroidism, chronic renal failure, severe liver disease).
  • Prolactinoma- diagnostic workup
  •  PRL
  •  FSH, LH, estradiol, progesterone (F)/ testosterone (M)
  • HyperPRL:
  • a) GnRH release-> ↓ LH secretion
  • b) Direct action on the ovary-> interference with LH and FSH signaling-> estradiol and
  • progesterone secretion and follicle maturation.
  •  Cortisol, ACTH, GH, IGF-1
  •  TSH, FT4
  •  Liver/ kidney function tests Differential diagnosis
  •  Pregnancy test (in women with amenorrhea)
  •  Imaging: MRI with contrast
  •  Visual Field Assessment

Hyperprolactinemia- treatment #6

  • 1. Treatment of the cause- whenever possible.
  • 2. First line treatment= Medical treatment with dopamine agonists:
  •  Bromocriptine (Parlodel®) 2.5 mg/tb; the dosage: 5–30 mg/day in divided doses.
  •  Cabergoline (Dostinex®) 0.5 mg/tb, 1/2–2 tb/day, twice/week.
  • Side effects: dizziness, postural hypotension, nausea, vomiting and cardiac valve disease (right-
  • sided cardiac fibrosis).
  • 3. Surgery= second line treatment for patients resistant/ intolerant of dopamine agonists.
  • Other indications:
  • • Pituitary apoplexy
  • • Prophylactic surgery (massive macroprolactinoma) before a planned pregnancy
  • 4. Radiotherapy-> prevents further tumor expansion
  • Diabetes insipidus- types and causes
  • 1. Central diabetes insipidus (lack of ADH)
  •  Craniopharyngiomas (the most common solid tumor to produce DI)
  •  Metastases, suprasellar pinealomas
  •  Surgery in the hypothalamic, pituitary stalk area
  •  Head trauma
  •  Infiltrative disorders: sarcoidosis, histiocytosis, lymphomas
  •  Infections: meningitis, meningoencephalitis
  •  Autoimmune
  •  DIDMOAD syndrome = DI + diabetes mellitus (DM) + optic atrophy + deafness
  •  Idiopathic
  • 2. Nephrogenic diabetes insipidus (lack of response to ADH in the collecting ducts- ADH
  • insensitive form)
  •  Chronic renal disease: any renal disease that interferes with collecting duct or
  • medullary function (e.g., chronic pyelonephritis, toxic nephritis, postobstructive
  • uropathy).
  •  Hypokalemia, hypercalcemia
  •  Drugs: lithium, demeclocycline

Diabetes insipidus- clinical picture #7

  • 1. Main features
  • - Adults: polyuria, polydipsia, nocturia.
  • - Children: polyuria, enuresis, failure to thrive.
  • 2. Other features
  • - Digestive manifestation: loss of appetite, weight loss, epigastric pain.
  • - Neuropsychiatric manifestations: headache, trouble sleeping (due to nocturia), fatigue.
  • - Dehydration signs: dry, pale skin, thirst, tachycardia, decrease in skin turgor.
  • Diabetes insipidus- diagnostic workup
  • I. Confirm LARGE URINE OUTPUT (>3 l/day), LOW URINARY SPECIFIC GRAVITY <1005,
  • LOW OSMOLALITY (<300 mOsm/kg).
  • II. Exclude other causes of polyuria- diabetes mellitus- glycemia, renal failure- renal
  • function rests, hypokalemia and hypercalcemia- electrolyte panel.
  • III. Fluid deprivation test: no fluids for 12–18 h-> in DI the result is abnormal: urine flow
  • remains increased, while urine specific gravity is less than 1005 and urine osmolality
  • remains <300 mOsm/kg; the patient becomes dehydrated.
  • !! This test can help distinguish DI from primary polyuria (greatly increased drinking >5
  • l/day-> functional inhibition of ADH secretion-> water diuresis)- the test will be normal in
  • primary polyuria.
  • IV. ADH radioimmunoassay (not routinely measured): Levels are low in central DI and high
  • in nephrogenic DI.
  • V. Vasopressin test (can help distinguish nephrogenic from central DI)- give 5 units of
  • vasopressin parenterally or 2 μg of desmopressin-> measure urinary flow, specific
  • gravity and osmolality:
  • a. In central DI : ↓ urinary flow and ↑ urinary specific gravity and osmolality
  • b. In nephrogenic DI : ↑ urinary flow and ↓ urinary specific gravity and osmolality
  • VI. Imagining- depending on the type of DI:
  • - Head MRI
  • !!May demonstrate loss of bright spot of the posterior pituitary gland.
  • - Abdominal ultrasound, intravenous urography: for the renal pathology.

Diabetes insipidus- differential diagnosis #8

  • 1. Primary polyuria
  • 2. Diabetes mellitus
  • 3. Hypokalemia and hypercalcemia
  • 4. Renal failure (the polyuric phase)
  • Diabetes insipidus- treatment
  • • Central Diabetes Insipidus
  • a) Hormonal treatment of substitution: DESMOPRESSIN ACETATE (Vasopressin analog,
  • acting predominantly on the V2 receptors in the kidney)-> divided doses (three
  • times/day)- orally (MINIRIN: 0.2–1.2 mg/day), intranasally, parenterally (SC, IV, IM),
  • sublingually.
  • Side effects: hyponatremia or hypo-osmolality
  • b) Etiologic treatment: the underlying disorder should be treated whenever possible!
  • • Nephrogenic Diabetes Insipidus
  • a) Correction of the underlying cause (metabolic or drugs).
  • b) High doses of desmopressin can be effective.
  • c) Maintenance of adequate fluid input.
  • d) HYDROCHLOROTHIAZIDE (NEFRIX) 25–50 mg/day + low sodium diet.
  • Hypopituitarism- pituitary causes
  •  Invasive- large pituitary adenoma, craniopharyngioma, metastatic lesions
  •  Infarction- spontaneous hemorrhagic infarction of a pituitary tumor= Pituitary apoplexy
  • (=MEDICAL EMERGENCY), ischemic pituitary necrosis=Sheehan syndrome (postpartum)
  •  Infiltrative- lymphoma, leukemia, histiocytosis X, hemochromatosis, sarcoidosis
  •  Injury- severe head trauma
  •  Immunologic- lymphocytic hypophysitis (autoimmune disorder)
  • Is  Iatrogenic- surgery, radiation of the pituitary gland
  •  Infectious- tuberculosis, syphilis, mycotic infections
  •  Isolated- genetic/ congenital causes (e.g. Kallmann syndrome- isolated defect in GnRH
  • secretion + hyposmia or anosmia)
  •  Idiopathic
  •  Empty sella

Hypopituitarism- clinical picture #9

  • !! Hypopituitarism classically develops in sequential order: GH-> FSH, LH-> TSH-> ACTH-> PRL
  •  GH Deficiency
  • Children: pituitary dwarfism- slow growth velocity, proportionate short stature (US/LS~1),
  • ↓ muscle mass, ↑ subcutaneous fat, immature facial appearance ( ), immature high-pitched
  • voice, delayed dental eruption, delayed bone age, normal IQ.
  • Adults: - clinically occult/fatigue, reduced exercise ability, ↓ quality of life
  • - decreased muscle mass, increased fat mass (abdominal and visceral), low bone mass
  • (osteoporosis), dry wrinkly skin; atherosclerosis, hyperlipidemia, insulin resistance
  •  Gonadotropin Deficiency
  • F: secondary amenorrhea, loss of axillary and pubic hair, breast and uterine atrophy and
  • decreased vaginal lubrication (dyspareunia)
  • M: decreased libido or erectile dysfunction, loss of the pubic and body hair, and testes atrophy
  • Hypopituitarism- clinical picture
  •  Thyrotropin Deficiency- the goiter is absent
  • - fatigue, apathy, nonpitting edema (e.g. eyelids, hands, feet), cold intolerance, dry,
  • pale skin, diurnal sleepiness, constipation, bradycardia, mental dullness, hoarseness
  •  Corticotropin Deficiency (“White” Addison)
  • - weakness, fatigue, depigmentation of the skin and ↓ tanning, arterial hypotension,
  • hypoglycemia, nausea, vomiting anorexia, weight loss
  •  PRL deficiency
  • - failure of lactation
  • Hypopituitarism- investigations
  • Basal tests of pituitary function:
  • - LH and FSH+ testosterone in males (9 a.m.)/ estradiol, progesterone in females
  • - GH, IGF-1, PRL
  • - TSH, FT4
  • - ACTH, cortisol (8-9 a.m.)
  • Dynamic (stimulation) tests- confirm the diagnosis and to assess the extent of hypofunction
  • - at present, these tests are not required in most patients, but they may be useful in
  • partial/mild pituitary insufficiency (e.g. low-normal TSH and low FT4).
  • Other Laboratory Findings
  • - anemia (thyroid and androgen deficiency and chronic disease), hypoglycemia,
  • hyponatremia (hypothyroidism and hypoadrenalism- inappropriate water retention)
  • Investigation of the cause
  • - Pituitary MRI, perimetry, and ophthalmoscopy- essential in confirming the existence
  • and defining the extent of the hypothalamic–pituitary lesion.

Pituitary dwarfism- diagnostic work-up #10

  • 1. Morphogram
  • 2. Basal tests
  • - IGF-1- ↓ (except for peripheral resistance to IGF-1 when the values are ↑)
  • - Basal values of serum GH are low in normal children and GH-deficient patients alike
  • -> the diagnosis of GH deficiency has classically rested on demonstration of an
  • inadequate rise of serum GH after provocative stimuli (dynamic tests)
  • 3. Dynamic tests
  • - With insulin (ITT), GHRH-arginine, clonidine, glucagon
  • - Normal response: GH should increase to a maximal level >7 ng/ml (children)/ >3
  • ng/ml (adults)
  • - For diagnosis: two different negative tests or one negative test+ ↓ IGF-1 are needed
  • 4. Evaluation of the pituitary reserve: FSH, LH, estradiol/testosterone, TSH/FT4,
  • ACTH/cortisol
  • 5. Radiographs of the left hand and wrist (bone age) → delayed bone age
  • 6. Pituitary MRI with contrast
  • Pituitary dwarfism- differential diagnosis
  • Endocrine causes Non-endocrine causes
  • - Hypothyroidism - Constitutional delay
  • - Precocious puberty - Achondroplasia
  • - Cushing’s - Turner syndrome
  • - Diabetes mellitus - Chronic illness (coeliac disease,
  • - Pseudohypoparathyroidism congenital heart disease, chronic
  • - Disorders of vitamin D renal failure, inflammatory bowel
  • metabolism disease, pulmonary disorders,
  • hematologic disorders)
  • Hypopituitarism- treatment
  • Involves - Adequate hormone replacement
  • - Management of the underlying cause
  • Therapeutic Principles
  •  The correction of the pituitary hormone deficits should be started conversely to their
  • classic course of onset
  •  Treatment for ACTH and TSH deficits are for life
  •  Usually performed by replacing the target hormone rather than the pituitary or
  • hypothalamic hormone. Exceptions: GH replacement and when fertility is desired

Hypopituitarism- treatment #11

  • 1.ACTH deficiency- glucocorticoid replacement only (mineralocorticoids usually not required)
  • - Hydrocortisone (15–25 mg/day) in 2–3 divided dose- most used
  • - alternative: Prednisone 5 mg/tb (5–7.5 mg/day orally) in 2–3 divided doses.
  • !! Increased dosage is required during periods of stress such as illness, surgery or trauma.
  • Monitoring: The clinical assessment is the most important, but biochemical monitoring, using
  • plasma and urine free cortisol may also be used.
  • 2.TSH deficiency
  • !!The adrenal disorder should be treated first (thyroid hormone replacement may aggravate
  • even partial adrenal insufficiency)
  • - Levothyroxine 50–150 μg/day (1.6 μg/kg/day)
  • Monitoring: clinical assessment+ measuring free thyroid hormone concentrations, which
  • should be in the middle upper part of the normal range (TSH can’t be used for monitoring).
  • Hypopituitarism- treatment
  • 3. FSH, LH deficiency
  • - Estrogen/testosterone administration is the usual method of replacement
  • F: estrogen for 21 days (e.g. oral/transdermal Estradiol) and progesterone for the last 10-12
  • days of estrogen therapy (e.g. Medroxyprogesterone)
  • M: testosterone replacement therapy- e.g. testosterone enanthate or cypionate (every 2
  • weeks- IM)/ testosterone undecanoate-Nebido (every 3 months- IM)/ testosterone patches
  • (daily application-transdermal)/ testosterone gels (daily application- transdermal)
  • !! Sexual hormone replacement therapy in children with coexisting GH and gonadotropin
  • deficiency may be started only after the target height is reached; otherwise-> advanced bone
  • age and epiphyseal fusion -> decrease in ultimate stature.
  • - Gonadotrophin therapy is required if fertility is desired!
  • Ovulation induction:
  •  Gonadal failure of hypothalamic origin- clomiphene citrate/ pulsatile subcutaneous
  • injections of GnRH with an infusion pump
  •  Gonadal failure of pituitary origin- combined treatment with recombinant FSH and LH
  • (hCG- chorionic gonadotropin)
  • Spermatogenesis
  •  Combined use of hCG and recombinant FSH
  •  Pulsatile GnRH infusion pumps

Hypopituitarism- treatment #12

  •  GH Deficiency
  • - replacement therapy with human GH produced by recombinant DNA technology
  • administered by daily SC injection- human biosynthetic somatropin (GENOTROPIN®,
  • NORDITROPIN®)
  • - Children : 25–75 μg/kg/day
  • - Adults: 2–5 μg/kg/day
  • Monitoring: clinical assessment + measurement of IGF-I.
  • Side effects: prepubertal gynecomastia, arthralgia, edema, benign intracranial hypertension,
  • insulin resistance, paresthesia, arrhythmias. Neoplasms are a concern (->counseling that
  • should include information about the unknown long-term risks of neoplasia).
  • Contraindications: diabetic retinopathy, active malignancy, intracranial hypertension.

Pituitary macroadenoma #13

  • Pituitary microadenoma
